title: Finite-kernel induction duality and negative-unipotent freeness
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $S$ be a semisimple simply connected affine $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme]: it is smooth, connected and of finite type, has no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, and every surjective homomorphism from a semisimple group scheme with finite central kernel to $S$ is an isomorphism. Solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes eventually become trivial; finite central means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra and commuting after every scalar extension. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subseteq B\subseteq S$ and a Borel subgroup $B$. A split torus is a product of copies of $\mathbf G_m$, with $\mathbf G_m(D)=D^\times$; maximal means maximal under inclusion; Borel means maximal smooth connected solvable closed subgroup. Its unipotent radical is its largest smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup, with unipotent meaning unipotent geometric matrices in a faithful representation. Use the character lattice $X^*(T)=\operatorname{Hom}(T,\mathbf G_m)$ and the positive roots $\Phi^+$ in the tangent space $\operatorname{Lie}(B)$, with roots interpreted as torus characters, as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Put $N=|\Phi^+|$. Fix $r\ge1$ and $q=p^r$. For each affine $F$-group $K$, put $K^{(q)}=\operatorname{Spec}(F[K]\otimes_{F,a\mapsto a^q}F)$ and $K_r=\ker(F^r_{K/F}:K\to K^{(q)})$, where the relative Frobenius has coordinate map $c\otimes a\mapsto ac^q$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. For a finite such kernel put $\operatorname{Dist}(K_r)=\operatorname{Hom}_F(F[K_r],F)$, with convolution product $(ab)(f)=(a\otimes b)(\Delta f)$, unit evaluation at the identity, augmentation $a\mapsto a(1)$ and antipode $\sigma$ dual to inversion; these agree with the finite-order distributions of [def-sfb-affine-group-distribution-calculus]. Let $\eta:T\to\mathbf G_m$ be any character and let $\widetilde\eta:B\to\mathbf G_m$ extend it, trivially on the unipotent radical. Define $L_r=(F^r_{S/F})^{-1}(T^{(q)})$, $P_r=B\cap L_r$, and
$$Z_r(\eta)=\{f\in F[L_r]:f(xb)=\widetilde\eta(b)f(x)\text{ for every commutative }F\text{-algebra }D,\ x\in L_r(D),\ b\in P_r(D)\}.$$
Equip this space with left translation $(h f)(x)=f(h^{-1}x)$. Rational modules and submodules mean counital coassociative coordinate coactions and linear subspaces stable under them. There exists a Borel subgroup $B^-$ containing $T$ with $B\cap B^-=T$. For every such opposite Borel, let $U^-$ be its unipotent radical. The kernels $S_r,B_r,U^-_r$ are finite group schemes. Set $A=\operatorname{Dist}(S_r)$, $D_B=\operatorname{Dist}(B_r)$, and $H=\operatorname{Dist}(U^-_r)$, viewed as subalgebras of $A$ by their closed inclusions. Let $F_\eta$ be the one-dimensional left $D_B$-module on which $b$ acts by $b(\widetilde\eta|_{B_r})$. Form the balanced tensor product
$$M_r(\eta)=A\otimes_{D_B}F_\eta,\qquad v_\eta=1\otimes1,$$
with its left $A$-action. Then $Z_r(\eta)$ is a rational $L_r$-module of dimension $q^N$. The map $H\to M_r(\eta)$, $h\mapsto hv_\eta$, is an isomorphism of left $H$-modules. Evaluation at the identity gives an $A$-linear isomorphism
$$\Theta_\eta:M_r(\eta)\xrightarrow{\sim}Z_r(\eta)^\vee,\qquad \Theta_\eta(a\otimes1)(f)=(\sigma(a)\cdot f)(1),$$
where $a\cdot f$ is obtained by applying $a$ to the restricted $S_r$-coaction and the dual action is $(a\ell)(f)=\ell(\sigma(a)f)$. In particular $v_\eta\ne0$. All assertions include $S=1$ and all primes, including $2$.

source.place: Agent formulation of finite-kernel PBW and evaluation duality, for the infinitesimal route to Jantzen II.3.18; general background I.8-I.9 and II.9.1. Local book WANTED; not asserted to have been inspected. Kaneda, Section 2.5, equations (4)-(6), printed p.322, corroborates the induction conventions but does not prove this precise duality statement.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], semisimplicity makes $S$ reductive. Put $U=R_u(B)$. By [lem-sfb-bruhat-longest-cell-charts], choose a longest representative $n_0$; then $n_0^2\in T(F)$ and $B_0^-=n_0Bn_0^{-1}$ satisfies $B\cap B_0^-=T$. Its radical is $U_0^-=n_0Un_0^{-1}$: conjugation preserves smoothness, connectedness, normality and unipotence, and carries the maximal subgroup with these properties to the maximal such subgroup. In particular $U,U_0^-\simeq\mathbf A_F^N$. The same Bruhat node gives the open immersion $(u,b)\mapsto un_0b$ with image $C_{w_0}$. Left translate by $n_0$. Since $n_0un_0b=(n_0un_0^{-1})(n_0^2b)$ and multiplication by $n_0^2$ is an automorphism of $B$, this produces the multiplication open immersion $U_0^-\times B\to S$. Denote its image by $C$; it contains $T$ (take the negative coordinate $1$).

source.place: 21.72, 21.80(b), 21.84--21.86, printed pp.447,450--452; explicit left translation of the cited Bruhat chart.

proof.text: This chart works for every opposite Borel in the statement. Indeed let $B^-\supseteq T$ satisfy $B\cap B^-=T$, and let $\Psi^+$ be its positive roots. By [lem-sfb-unipotent-root-intersection-products], the intersection has the product coordinates $(\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+\cap\Psi^+}U_\alpha)\times T$. Every root factor is an affine line by [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. Thus the intersection can equal $T$ only if $\Phi^+\cap\Psi^+=\varnothing$ (a nonempty product would have tangent dimension strictly larger than that of $T$). The positive-system assertion of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], applied also to $B^-$ and $B_0^-$, says that each positive system contains exactly one of each pair $\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$. Their positive roots therefore both equal $-\Phi^+$. By [lem-sfb-borel-root-product-coordinates], their radicals are the images of the identical ordered product of the same negative root subgroups, so $U^-=U_0^-$. Finally $B^-=U^-T=B_0^-$ by the semidirect-product assertion of the Borel-pair node. We henceforth use $C=U^-B$ for this arbitrary opposite.

source.place: 21.68(a), 21.84--21.86, printed pp.445,451--452; expanded uniqueness argument from the cited intersection and product statements.

proof.text: Write $\operatorname{Fr}_K=F^r_{K/F}$. Its given coordinate formula proves naturality and compatibility with products: for a coordinate homomorphism $\varphi$ one has $\varphi(c^q)=\varphi(c)^q$, and $(a\otimes b)^q=a^q\otimes b^q$. Applied to group multiplication this proves $\operatorname{Fr}_S(uv)=\operatorname{Fr}_{U^-}(u)\operatorname{Fr}_B(v)$ in the twisted multiplication chart $C^{(q)}$. There is no assertion that this product chart is a group homomorphism. Since $F$ is algebraically closed, $a\mapsto a^q$ is an automorphism. If $I\subset F[S]$ is the ideal of $T$, the ideal of $L_r$ is generated by $i^q$ for $i\in I$. Its radical is $I$, because $F[T]$ is reduced. Hence $|L_r|=|T|\subset C$, and the closed subscheme $L_r$ factors through the open $C$. The same calculation for the identity ideal shows $|S_r|=\{1\}\subset C$. These conclusions retain the nonreduced scheme structures; only containment in the open is tested topologically.

source.place: 2.25--2.28, printed pp.47--48; agent calculation with the explicitly defined relative Frobenius coordinate map and the big cell from steps 1--2.

proof.text:
In $C^{(q)}\simeq(U^-)^{(q)}\times B^{(q)}$, the torus $T^{(q)}$ consists of pairs $(1,t)$; the identity consists of $(1,1)$. The multiplication chart and the formula of step 3 therefore give, as fibre products of schemes,
$$U^-_r\times P_r\xrightarrow{\sim}L_r,\quad(u,b)\mapsto ub,\qquad U^-_r\times B_r\xrightarrow{\sim}S_r,\quad(u,b)\mapsto ub.$$
Explicitly, in the chart $\operatorname{Fr}_S(ub)\in T^{(q)}$ is equivalent to $\operatorname{Fr}_{U^-}(u)=1$ and $\operatorname{Fr}_B(b)\in T^{(q)}$, the latter saying precisely $b\in B\cap L_r=P_r$. For the identity fibre it is equivalent to both Frobenius images being $1$. These are equations of morphisms, hence hold on every test algebra, not only on field-valued points. Right multiplication by $P_r$ acts on the first product by $(u,b)c=(u,bc)$, and left multiplication by $U^-_r$ acts by $v(u,b)=(vu,b)$.

source.place: 2.27--2.28 and 21.84--21.86, printed pp.48,451--452; agent fibre-product calculation in the multiplication chart.

proof.text:
Choose the affine-space coordinates on $U$ and $U^-$ from step 1, translating them so that the identity has all coordinates zero. Naturality of Frobenius with respect to these scheme isomorphisms gives
$$F[U_r]\simeq F[t_1,\ldots,t_N]/(t_1^q,\ldots,t_N^q),\qquad F[U^-_r]\simeq F[z_1,\ldots,z_N]/(z_1^q,\ldots,z_N^q).$$
The monomials with every exponent between $0$ and $q-1$ form bases: reduce each exponent modulo the monomial ideal, in which all other monomials and no linear combination of the retained monomials lie. Thus both coordinate algebras have dimension $q^N$. If $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^s$, then $F[T_r]=F[y_1^{\pm1},\ldots,y_s^{\pm1}]/(y_i^q-1)_i$ has basis $\prod_i y_i^{a_i}$, $0\le a_i<q$, and dimension $q^s$. The semidirect product $B=U\rtimes T$ from [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], by the same product-fibre calculation as step 4, gives $B_r\simeq U_r\times T_r$. Step 4 now makes all three kernels finite. Their augmentation ideals are generated by the displayed nilpotent variables and $y_i-1$; a product of more than the sum of their maximal exponents vanishes. Thus their full coordinate duals are indeed finite-order distributions in [def-sfb-affine-group-distribution-calculus].

source.place: 2.25--2.28, pp.47--48; 21.84--21.86, pp.451--452; agent monomial calculation, valid for every q=p^r.

proof.text:
Put $C_-=F[U^-_r]$ and $C_B=F[B_r]$. The second isomorphism of step 4 identifies $F[S_r]$ with $C_-\otimes C_B$. Choose their finite bases $c_i,d_j$ and coefficient functionals $h_i,b_j$. The transpose of multiplication sends $h_i\otimes b_j$ to the functional extracting the coefficient of $c_i\otimes d_j$. These are exactly the dual basis, so multiplication gives a vector-space isomorphism
$$m:H\otimes_FD_B\xrightarrow{\sim}A,\qquad h\otimes b\mapsto hb.$$
Indeed convolution gives $(hb)(f)=(h\otimes b)(f(uv))$, the transpose just described. The inclusions into $A$ are injective because restriction of coordinate functions along closed inclusions is surjective, and the dual of a surjection is injective (evaluate after a preimage). They preserve product and unit by the same multiplication and identity formulas. Associativity shows $m(h'h\otimes bb')=h'm(h\otimes b)b'$; thus $m$ is also an isomorphism of left $H$, right $D_B$ bimodules. All these assertions use scheme multiplication, not a nonexistent product group law on the chart.

source.place: Agent finite-basis transpose calculation from step 4 and the convolution formula in the item; background 2.30 and Definition 3.3, printed pp.49,65--66.

proof.text:
Write $\chi(b)=b(\widetilde\eta|_{B_r})$. The character equation $\Delta(\widetilde\eta)=\widetilde\eta\otimes\widetilde\eta$ gives $\chi(bb')=\chi(b)\chi(b')$ and $\chi(1)=1$. Under $m$ of step 6, the balanced relation in $A\otimes_{D_B}F_\eta$ is
$$(h\otimes bb')\otimes t=(h\otimes b)\otimes\chi(b')t.$$
Consequently $h\mapsto h\otimes_{D_B}1$ has inverse $(\sum_i h_i b_i)\otimes_{D_B}t\mapsto\sum_i h_i\chi(b_i)t$. This formula is independent of the displayed sum because $m^{-1}$ is a linear map, and respects every balanced relation by the multiplicativity of $\chi$. The two compositions are identities, the second using $(hb)\otimes1=h\otimes\chi(b)$. This proves the required left $H$-module isomorphism $H\simeq M_r(\eta)$, with $1_H$ corresponding to $v_\eta$.

source.place: Agent balanced-tensor calculation from step 6; no induction/coinduction duality theorem is assumed.

proof.text: Let $C_L=F[L_r]$ and write $\Omega:C_L\to C_L\otimes F[P_r]$ for $f\mapsto\rho_R(f)-f\otimes\widetilde\eta$, where $\rho_R(f)(x,b)=f(xb)$. The corrected all-test-algebras covariance condition is exactly $Z_r(\eta)=\ker\Omega$. Left translation is the regular coaction $c(f)(x,h)=f(h^{-1}x)$. It commutes with right translation since $(h^{-1}x)b=h^{-1}(xb)$. Thus $(\Omega\otimes1)c(f)=0$ if $\Omega(f)=0$. Write $c(f)=\sum_i f_i\otimes a_i$ with the finitely many $a_i$ linearly independent; applying their coefficient functionals gives $\Omega(f_i)=0$ for each $i$. Therefore $c$ restricts to $Z_r(\eta)\to Z_r(\eta)\otimes C_L$. Its counit and coassociativity identities are inherited from left translation on $C_L$. This is precisely the rational module convention of [def-sfb-affine-group-distribution-calculus]. The same calculation works over every algebra extension, including nonreduced ones.

source.place: Agent commuting-coactions calculation; Kaneda Section 2.3, printed p.320, corroborates left regular action and evaluation conventions (read online; local paper WANTED).

proof.text:
By the first product chart of step 4, restriction to $U^-_r$ gives a linear isomorphism
$$Z_r(\eta)\xrightarrow{\sim}F[U^-_r],\qquad f\mapsto g=f|_{U^-_r}.$$
Its inverse is the regular function $f(ub)=g(u)\widetilde\eta(b)$ on $L_r\simeq U^-_r\times P_r$. It has the required covariance because $\widetilde\eta(bc)=\widetilde\eta(b)\widetilde\eta(c)$; conversely covariance with $x=u$ forces that formula for every $f\in Z_r(\eta)$. Both formulas are identities of coordinate functions, as checked on the universal test algebra, and their compositions are the identity since $\widetilde\eta(1)=1$. Hence $\dim_F Z_r(\eta)=\dim_F F[U^-_r]=q^N$ by step 5.

source.place: Agent coordinate proof using steps 4--5; compare Kaneda Section 2.5, printed p.322, the opposite-kernel product preceding equation (4), read online.

proof.text:
Let $e(f)=f(1)$. Inversion squared is the identity, so its transpose satisfies $\sigma^2=1$; the inverse of a product reverses its factors, so $\sigma(ab)=\sigma(b)\sigma(a)$. For any distribution $a\in A$ and $f\in Z_r(\eta)$ the left-translation convention gives
$$(\sigma(a)\cdot f)(1)=a(f|_{S_r}),$$
because both the left action and $\sigma$ insert inversion, which cancels. For $b\in D_B$, covariance at $1$ gives $f|_{B_r}=e(f)\widetilde\eta|_{B_r}$, so $e(\sigma(b)f)=\chi(b)e(f)$. Define $\theta(a)(f)=e(\sigma(a)f)$. Since $\sigma(a)f$ is again in $Z_r(\eta)$ by step 8, we get $\theta(ab)=\chi(b)\theta(a)$. Thus $a\otimes1\mapsto\theta(a)$ respects the balanced relation and defines $\Theta_\eta$. Finally
$$\Theta_\eta(ca\otimes1)(f)=e(\sigma(a)\sigma(c)f)=(c\,\Theta_\eta(a\otimes1))(f).$$
This proves $A$-linearity for exactly the dual action stated in the item; in particular the character in $F_\eta$ has not been replaced by its inverse.

source.place: Agent antipode and evaluation calculation; Kaneda Section 2.3(5)--(6), printed pp.320--321, corroborates evaluation and the inverse in the left regular action, read online.

proof.text:
Under $H\simeq M_r(\eta)$ from step 7 and $Z_r(\eta)\simeq C_-$ from step 9, the last displayed identity of step 10 gives
$$\Theta_\eta(hv_\eta)(f)=h(f|_{U^-_r}).$$
This is the ordinary perfect pairing between the finite-dimensional coordinate space $C_-$ and its full dual $H$. More explicitly, take the truncated monomial basis $z^\alpha$ of step 5, its coefficient dual $h_\alpha$, and extend $z^\alpha$ to the unique $f_\alpha\in Z_r(\eta)$ of step 9. Then $\Theta_\eta(h_\alpha v_\eta)(f_\beta)=\delta_{\alpha\beta}$, so its matrix is the identity and $\Theta_\eta$ is bijective. Also $1_H\ne0$ since $1_H(1)=1$, and step 7 gives $v_\eta\ne0$. When $S=1$ all coordinate products are empty, $N=0$, $H=A=D_B=F$ and these maps are the identity on a one-dimensional space. Every argument used only $q=p^r$ and polynomial coefficients; no factorial or scalar divisible by $p$ was inverted, so $p=2$ and every $r\ge1$ are included.

source.place: Agent dual-basis verification from steps 5,7,9--10; this proves the evaluation isomorphism rather than invoking a separate finite-kernel duality result.

reviewed.note: mechanical checks by tools/merge_delivery.py; mathematics reviewed in full by NT-cc-Q120-5ce720a4e (reviewer sub-agent of L); spot-checked: I read the item in full: 11 steps, no new nodes, no fixes. (2) Every opposite Borel equals n0 B n0^-1: the intersection node with empty Phi+ cap Psi+, the positive-system property and the root-product node give equal radicals.
